newsitem.title: USA: Perot should not be in U.S. election debates - panel.
newsitem.headline: Perot should not be in U.S. election debates - panel.

text.p: A commission planning for the 1996 presidential debates recommended on Tuesday that Reform Party candidate Ross Perot be excluded from debates between President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole.

"The commission unanimously agreed with the unanimous recommendation of our independent advisory committee that only President Clinton and Senator Dole and their running mates be invited to participate," commission co-chairmen Paul Kirk and Frank Fahrenkopf said in a statement.

"Our decision ... was made on the basis that only President Clinton and Senator Dole have a realistic chance as set forth in our criteria to be elected the next president of the United States," the statement said.

The bipartisan panel said it could reconsider its decision for later debates -- three or four are in prospect -- if Perot improved his weak position in opinion polls. Surveys show him with only five to eight percent support this year.
The decision was a victory for Dole, who feared the participation of Perot in the widely-watched televised debates would siphon votes from him rather than Clinton.

Four years ago, when Perot played a prominent role in the debates and went on to win about 19 percent of the popular vote, many Republicans claimed he took votes away from then-President George Bush and helped elect Democrat Clinton.

Dole spokesman Nelson Warfield said the decision "makes it a hell of a lot more likely" that the Republican candidate will win the election. And Dole, whoi is struggling badly in the polls, said on his arrival in Phoenix, Arizona for a campaign event that the debates should start quickly.
"I think the debates ought to begin, the 25th, 26th of this month rather than trying to crowd them all into October, Dole told reporters at Phoenix airport.
"I want to reach out to the Perot supporters ... I think we (Republicans) are the Reform party," Dole said.

The first debate had tentatively been scheduled for September 25 but Clinton asked for a delay because he is speaking to the United Nations General Assembly the day before and wanted more time to prepare for both appearances.
Clinton had wanted Perot included in the debates, and his campaign debate negotiator, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, said: "We regret the Commission's decision."
At a campaign stop in Westland, Michigan, Clinton said he had enjoyed debating Perot in 1992. Asked whether he was worried about debating Dole one-on-one, he said: "I'm not afraid of any debate."
Perot supporters were angry at the recommendation. Russell Verney, National Coordinator of the Perot campaign, called it a "travesty."
Verney said the Reform party was considering going to federal court in an attempt to get Perot into the debates.

Negotiators for Dole and Clinton met after the announcement of the decision on Tuesday to discuss how the debates should proceed. The two candidates do not have to accept the commission recommendation and a Clinton campaign official said that the Perot matter was "still on the table."

In 1992, Texas billionaire Perot ran as an independent candidate financing his own presidential campaign and took part in the debates. His third-placed election finish was one of the strongest by a third-force challenger in U.S. history.

This year, he formed his own Reform Party and named maverick economist Pat Choate as his running mate. On the basis of his strong 1992 showing, Perot qualified for $29.2 million in federal money to finance his 1996 run for the White House.
So far, however, Perot has garnered only single-digit support in opinion polls that place Clinton and Dole far ahead of him and Clinton well out front of Dole.
The debates have become highlights of the presidential election seasons and a record 97 million Americans watched the final 1992 televised debate.
